newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed mostly higher following the steadier New York market and news of a port strike in key grower Colombia. January finished $10 higher at $1,355 per tonne while March added $17 to close at $1,330 per tonne. Turnover reached an impressive 8,112 lots centered on March and May contracts. News LIFE certified stocks fell by 226 to 1,875 5-tonne lots in December had little impact as it was in line with earlier expectations. In New York arabica futures closed moderately higher with front month March adding 40 points to close at 122.60 cents/lb. May closed 15 points higher at 119.00 cents/lb.

The rise was prompted by reports of a strike in Colombia as well as follow through buying from yesterday. A strike by Colombian dock workers has paralysed the 60 per cent of the country's coffee exports that are shipped out through the Pacific coast port of Buenaventura. Traders said the strike has halted loading of 90,000 bags of coffee destined for export. The dock strike was declared late Tuesday and began to bite Wednesday. Officials declined to speculate on the duration of the strike but said it would not be easy to divert shipments destined for export to the Caribbean coast ports, which currently handle about 40 percent of Colombia's exports. A longer strike could have a noticeable impact on world market prices.

After the close the Green Coffee Association of New York reported an increase in US warehouse stocks in December by 63,000 60-kg bags to 1.327 million bags. Although this was in line with expectations it could have a mildly negative impact which, however, could be offset by the strike in Colombia. The port of Laredo, Texas, posted the largest gain in coffee stocks, presumably Mexican coffee coming in. Further price development will very much depend whether or not the strike in Colombia will continue.

UNITED STATES - Supplies of green coffee stocks housed in US warehouses rose in December 1996 by 63,000 60-kg bags to 1.327 million bags, the Green Coffee Association of New York said. The port of Laredo, Texas, posted the largest gain in coffee stocks with 69,000 bags to 173,000 bags, the GCA said. Inventories increased by 52,000 bags, to 204,000 bags in New York. However, warehouse stocks in New Orleans decreased in December, falling 48,000 bags to 481,000 bags.
UNITED KINGDOM - Certified coffee stocks fell 229 5-tonne lots to 1,875 lots in December from 2,104 lots in November, the exchange said. The drop was in line with earlier expectations.

KENYA - Aggrey Ole Murunga, general manager of the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK), told Reuters that coffee production in 1996/97 (October/September) is likely to fall to below 1.5 million 60-kg bags, down from 1.626 million bags in 1995/96. Our most recent estimate for 1996/97 was 1.416 million bags. Murunga blamed coffee berry disease in a number of key growing districts as well as poor weather in others for the setback in production. Murunga put exports in 1995/96 at 1.823 million bags, up from 1.325 million bags the previous year.
TAIWAN - Taiwan imported 172,700 bags of coffee in January/October 1996. The country imports most of its coffee in the form of solubles. Main suppliers are Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and Singapore.

HONG KONG - Hong Kong imported 147,800 bags of coffee in January/October 1996, 12 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar 1995 dropped sharply by 35 percent to 156,400 bags. The country gets most of its coffee in the form of solubles from the United States, China and South Korea. Exports in January/October 1996 fell by 49 percent to 51,100 bags. Already last year exports were sharply down at 120,500 bags from 227,100 bags the previous year.
